Where should the majlis and family living room go on a villa floor plan?

By Wael Bousmael · Published 28 November 2026

Picture an evening when guests arrive for dinner just as someone gets home from football. Which door does each person use? Put a copy of the ground-floor plan on the table and walk through that evening. It will tell you which rooms belong together and where you need a door you can close.

Can the majlis share the family entrance?

Use one colour to trace a guest from the gate to a seat in the majlis, the room where you receive visitors. Use another to trace a family member from the car to the stairs. If you like greeting each other at the door, a shared hall with two onward routes may suit you. If the family wants to come and go independently, draw a separate entrance and check where the paths next meet.

What can a guest see on the way to the washbasin?

Mark the majlis doorway and the guest washbasin. Follow the route between them with the kitchen and living room doors drawn open. Does the family sofa come into full view? On a second copy, move the majlis doorway along the wall or give the entrance a turn before the living room. Compare the view from the guest route in each version.

Walk a dinner tray from the kitchen to the table

Draw the dining table and chairs, with one chair pulled out as if a guest were sitting in it. Trace a tray from the kitchen to the table, then take the empty plates back. If the route crosses between the sofa and the television or clips the occupied chair, try turning the table or moving the dining room door before asking for a bigger room.

Give your architect one specific note on the drawing

Circle a crossing you would like to avoid and write what happens there in your household. For example, “We host Friday dinner and want the children to reach the kitchen from the stairs while guests are in the majlis.” Your architect can draw another layout, and you can test it against the same evening.
